main_point: Swedish police raided The Pirate Bay and Piratbyrån on copyright violation grounds, sparking debate over the legality of the site, the involvement of US media corporations, and the lawfulness of seizing unrelated servers.

aliases: head of the Swedish Pirate Party
CEO of the Motion Picture Association of America

statements.text: The Swedish National Criminal Police launched an operation against the servers of The Pirate Bay and Piratbyrån. This Swedish lobby group created the website. The police used 50 officers for the raid. They acted because of suspected copyright violations.
statements.text_short: Swedish law enforcement officers conducted a search of The Pirate Bay and Piratbyrån servers, acting on reports of possible copyright breaches.

statements.text: Swedish officials have launched raids against The Pirate Bay and Piratbyrån, claiming copyright infringement. This move comes as a shock because the site's legal status has been debated openly for more than three years. During this time, the operators often released press statements arguing that these actions are not lawful.
statements.text_short: The raid on The Pirate Bay is surprising given the site's long-standing public debate over its legality.

actor_aliases: head of the Swedish Pirate Party
statements.text: Rickard Falkvinge, who leads the Swedish Pirate Party, stated that law enforcement detained three employees of The Pirate Bay. However, only two individuals were actually held in custody. This gap indicates a difference between the original arrest warrants and the final results regarding who was taken into custody.
statements.text_short: Rickard Falkvinge stated that law enforcement detained three employees, but only two individuals were actually placed in custody.

actor_aliases: CEO of the Motion Picture Association of America
statements.text: Dan Glickman, who leads the Motion Picture Association of America, praised the Swedish police operation against The Pirate Bay. He stated this action shows that copyright thieves have no safe havens. The MPAA also claims the website provided more than 150,000 files, which included major summer blockbusters.
statements.text_short: Dan Glickman, who works for the MPAA, praised the raid. He said this shows that copyright thieves have no safe harbors.

statements.text: The Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA) designates The Pirate Bay as a primary target for enforcement, asserting that the site distributes over 150,000 files, including major Hollywood blockbusters, thereby justifying aggressive action against it as a hub for copyright infringement.
statements.text_short: The MPAA identifies The Pirate Bay as a top copyright infringement target hosting major blockbusters.

statements.text: The Pirate Bay asserts that it operates as the world's largest BitTorrent tracker, a claim that underscores its role as a central distribution point for digital content regardless of whether the hosted files are copyrighted or freely licensed.
statements.text_short: The Pirate Bay states that it is the biggest BitTorrent tracker on the planet.

statements.text: The Pirate Bay distinguishes the current police raid from a similar event one year prior, clarifying that the previous incident was merely a routine server update rather than a publicity stunt, and noting that the current seizure of unrelated private servers lacks a clear legal basis.
statements.text_short: The Pirate Bay clarifies the current raid is not a publicity stunt and questions the legality of seizing unrelated servers.

statements.text: Swedish officials have confirmed the authenticity of the police raid on The Pirate Bay, which was followed by a site notice promising restoration within days, while the site's owner was arrested and interrogated without access to a public defender or legal representation.
statements.text_short: Officials confirm the raid's authenticity, noting the arrest of the site owner without legal representation.

statements.text: Swedish authorities informed the owner of the hosting company that they were not required to assign a public defender to him, arguing that the copyright charges he faced did not carry a potential prison sentence. This decision to withhold legal representation was made despite the fact that the raid had also resulted in the seizure of private servers belonging to unrelated customers, raising concerns about the proportionality of the law enforcement actions.
statements.text_short: Swedish police denied the right to a public defender for a hosting owner, citing the non-custodial nature of the copyright charges.
